demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He tells me the story in fragments, never looking at me directly. He's a dancer-was a dancer, he corrects himself-with a company for thirty years. Fifty-six years old, still lean and quick, but now he sits in my office with his hands pressed flat on his thighs, as if holding himself in place. He came because his wife said she couldn't watch him disappear anymore.

The event happened eighteen months ago, during a rehearsal for a contemporary piece. He was partnered with a younger dancer, a woman named Elena. The choreography called for a lift where he would catch her from a turn and lower her into a backward arc. He had done it a hundred times. But this time his timing was off-a half-second delay, a misjudgment of her momentum. She twisted in the air, and he caught her wrong. He heard a sound he describes as a wet branch snapping. Her spine. She fell, and then she screamed. He held her until the ambulance came, her body limp and wrong in his arms.

She survived, but she will not walk again. He knows her name, her hometown, the color of her daughter's hair. He has never seen her since the hospital. He cannot bring himself to call.

In the sessions since, I have watched the details emerge slowly, like blood through a bandage. He tells me that for the first few months after the accident, he kept dancing. He went to rehearsals, took class, performed. But his body began to refuse. His hands would tremble before a lift. His peripheral vision would snag on any sudden movement. Once, during a run-through, a lighting technician dropped a sandbag across the stage, and he dove to the floor, covering his head, heart pounding so hard he thought he was dying. The company gave him a leave of absence. He has not set foot in a studio since.

Now he wakes at three or four each morning, drenched, the sound of her scream ringing in his ears. Sometimes he hears the snap. He lies beside his wife, who sleeps with her back to him now-not out of anger, he says, but out of exhaustion. She has tried. She has held him through nightmares, coaxed him to eat, suggested therapy. He knows he is lucky to have her. But when she reaches for him, he feels a chasm opening between them, a space filled with the image of Elena's face as she fell.

He avoids mirrors. He avoids motion. He avoids the music he once loved-any rhythmic pattern, any melodic rise, because it pulls at his limbs, and his limbs remember what they did. At his worst, he stands in his kitchen for an hour, unable to decide how to pour a glass of water. The simplest movement feels freighted with consequence.

He has not told anyone this, but he replays the moment every day, adjusting the variables: if he had shifted his weight sooner, if he had opened his hands differently, if he had called out a warning. In these revisions, Elena is always fine. She laughs, takes her bow, walks off stage. And he is free. But then reality crashes back, and he feels the guilt like a physical weight-a cold metallic taste in his mouth, a pressure behind his sternum.

His PCL-5 score of 62 reflects what I already see: the relentless intrusions, the avoidance of dance and social contact, the negative thoughts about himself (killer, monster, failure), the hypervigilance that makes him scan every room for sharp edges and fast-moving objects. He is not sleeping. He is not dancing. He is not sure there is a person left underneath the shame.

He told me, last week, in a voice so quiet I had to lean forward: "I used to feel beautiful when I moved. Now I only feel dangerous."
